subject: Art & Design
title: Monet and the Birth of Impressionism
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Monet and the Birth of Impressionism.

hook.text: A critic meant 'Impression' as an insult. Monet and friends adopted it as their name.

buildup.text: Impressionists painted outdoors, fast, capturing how light changed minute by minute.

discovery.text: They used visible brushstrokes and pure color side by side instead of mixing on a palette.

twist.text: The Salon rejected them. So they organized their own exhibition — and art was never the same.

climax.text: Monet painted the same haystack 25 times at different hours to prove light is the real subject.

punchline.text: They didn't paint things. They painted light hitting things.

quiz.question: What was the Impressionists' key innovation?
options: Capturing fleeting effects of natural light with visible brushstrokes
Painting only indoors with artificial light

details.summary: Claude Monet (1840-1926) painted outdoors to capture fleeting effects of light on water, haystacks, and cathedrals. His painting 'Impression, Sunrise' (1872) accidentally named the movement when a critic used 'Impressionist' as an insult.
details.whyItMatters: Impressionism broke art free from the studio and academic rules. By painting what the eye actually sees — shimmering light, dissolved edges, vibrant color — Monet launched modern art's obsession with perception over narration.
takeaways: Painted outdoors to capture fleeting light effects
Late water lily paintings anticipated abstract art

faq.question: Why were the Impressionists rejected by the art establishment?
faq.answer: Their loose brushwork, bright colors, and everyday subjects violated academic standards demanding smooth finish, muted tones, and historical subjects. Critics called their work unfinished sketches. The artists organized their own exhibitions after repeated Salon rejections.

faq.question: Why did Monet paint the same subjects repeatedly?
faq.answer: He was painting light, not objects. His series of haystacks, Rouen Cathedral, and water lilies show the same subject at different times and seasons, proving that what we see is mostly shifting light and atmosphere rather than fixed physical form.
